The daughter is the one hearing the smartphone call; her father is the hostage whose life is being begged for, and the kidnapper is demanding that she bring one hundred million yen alone by noon. She decides not to pay because the father himself is already physically restrained or captive in a way that makes the ransom demand impossible for her to satisfy—specifically, the father is being held hostage, so she cannot simply deliver money to save him as demanded. Her refusal is therefore based on the impossibility of complying with the kidnapper’s conditions, not on believing the call is fake or on lacking the money.

The father is the hostage whose life is being begged for, but he is also the person hearing the demand and deciding not to pay it. He is already physically restrained or captive—held hostage—when he hears the kidnapper’s smartphone demand for one hundred million yen. Because he is bound and unable to go anywhere, he cannot comply with the instruction to bring the money alone by noon. His decision not to pay therefore rests on the impossibility of making the delivery himself, rather than on the ransom being fake, the money being unavailable, or a police operation.
